**The Impact of Pre- Service Language Teachers' Basic Psychological Needs on Behavioural Intentions to Utilise Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Teaching: AI Literacy and Self- Efficacy as Mediators**

**Correspondence:** Xia Siquan ([qd702277@163.com)](mailto:qd702277@163.com) **Received:** 24 June 2024 \| **Revised:** 7 May 2025 \| **Accepted:** 16 June 2025

**Funding:** The authors received no specific funding for this work. **Keywords:** AI literacy \| behavioural intentions \| pre- service language teachers \| self- determination theory (SDT)

## ABSTRACT Grounded in Self- Determination Theory (SDT), this study investigates how pre- service language teachers' psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relevance) influence their behavioural intentions to adopt AI, with AI literacy and self- efficacy as me- diators. Structural equation modelling analysis of 562 Chinese pre- service language teachers revealed that satisfaction of psy- chological needs exerts a substantial and positive effect on behavioural intentions to utilise AI, which is mediated by AI literacy and self- efficacy. In particular, the perceived autonomy, relevance and competence of pre- service teachers are deemed to exert profound influence on AI literacy and AI self- efficacy. The direct effect of autonomy and relevance on behavioural intentions is significant, whereas competence fails to exert a direct influence on behavioural intentions. This suggests that, through AI literacy, the satisfaction of competence can indirectly influence behavioural intentions to employ new technologies such as AI. These findings underscore the necessity of integrating psychological empowerment and technical competence cultivation in AI training programmes, offering actionable insights for fostering AI- integrated language education.

As early as 1989, Davis  (1989) discussed several factors that influence teachers' behavioural intentions in their use of tech- nology teaching systems, such as underlining the role of per- ceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) in technology acceptance. With the advent of AI technology, tra- ditional technical models have also emerged in recent years. For example, Yao and wang (2024) have evaluated factors that affect pre- service special education teachers' behavioural in- tentions for AI education, comprising digital literacy, teacher self- efficacy, perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness. These studies demonstrated the universal validity of existing technology- related models such as the technology acceptance model (TAM), and planned behaviour theory (TPB) investiga- tions and identified some predictors bound up with teachers' be- havioural intentions to employ AI. Although existing research models shed light upon the relevant factors of the behavioural intentions of AI technology, most of them center around exter- nal technical attributes (such as perceived usefulness and ease of use), take into account the technical object from objective conditions, while it from the user's subjective standpoint, that is, they ignore the internal psychological motivation of teach- ers' behavioural intentions of using AI technology. Hence, in recent years, new viewpoints have also emerged to explore the rich research on behavioural intentions by technological learn- ing and using behavioural intentions, namely the innate needs (autonomy, competence and relevance) in SDT, which serves as the core framework for explaining human motivations, un- derlining that behavioural intentions are driven by the satis- faction of three basic psychological needs, namely, autonomy (i.e., dominant perception of action choice), sense of competence (confidence about one's efficacy), and relevance (interacting be- longing with groups or environments) (Ryan and Deci 2020). Chai et al. (2022) research uses SDT theory to throw light upon students' behavioural intentions to learn AI. Chai et al. (2022) also come up with a viewpoint that there is limited research on the impact on teachers' learning and application of AI technol- ogy from the viewpoint of demand satisfaction. In the AI era, more SDT- based teachers need to continue their motivational research, which echoes the recent call from the founder of SDT (Ryan and Deci 2017, 2020).

On that account, considering the identity characteristics of pre- service teachers as research objects, they are not dissimilar from the student identity of continuous learning, nor are they in- service teachers with certain technical experience and means, and face dual social pressure (technical adaptation + role trans- formation) (Abedi et al. 2024), and in response to the sensitive period of pre- service teachers' ability needs (such as urgently needing to master the principles of AI technology) and the anx- iety period of belonging (such as worrying about AI threatening professional authority), a differentiated path to technology use behavioural intentions that focus on the psychological needs of pre- service teachers.

Contemporary studies have underscored that behavioural inten- tions are determined not solely by technical features but also in- trinsically linked to users' psychological needs and motivational 

dynamics (Pan 2020). The complexity of AI technology and the diversity of educational scenarios require users to possess cor- responding technical capabilities (AI literacy) and confidence (self- efficacy).

Aside from that, empirical evidence further suggests that knowl- edge deficits constrain teachers' confidence in using technology, with this lack of confidence emerging as the primary barrier to technology adoption behaviours (Seo et al. 2021). In this case, it can be appropriately inferred that although psychological mo- tivations (such as autonomy, competence and relevance) drive behavioural intentions under the SDT theoretical framework. Furthermore, their effects on complex behaviours in technical contexts (such as AI technology applications) may be limited by the competence and confidence of users. AI literacy, central to educators' competence to navigate AI technology challenges, is bound up with their behavioural intentions. By satisfying indi- viduals' basic psychological needs (such as autonomy and com- petence) under the SDT framework, self- efficacy and AI literacy can become pivotal mediators between psychological needs and behavioural intentions.

To sum up, this study introduces the SDT framework for the con- struction of a new mediation model that combines psychologi- cal needs, self- efficacy, AI literacy and behavioural intentions. Unlike the traditional Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this integrated framework not only addresses technological at- tributes but also, from a psychological motivation standpoint, clarifies how educators' AI adoption is mediated through the transformation of their knowledge and skills into psychological need fulfilment. Indeed, this model not only provides deeper theoretical support for understanding the complex acceptance process of AI technology, but also offers pivotal guidance for the design of teacher training programs.

**2 \| Literature Review and Research Questions**

**2.1 \| The Application of AI in Language Teaching**

AI's rapid emergence and evolution has greatly impacted the field of language acquisition. AI is progressively recognised as a pivotal driver of innovation and transformation in language educat (Ye 2025). It boasts enormous capacity to strengthen lan- guage learning settings by offering automated feedback, intelli- gent tutoring and personalised learning experiences (Weng and Chiu 2022). The operation and functionality of AI in language education can be delineated into three crucial dimensions. To start with, AI leverages machine learning algorithms to probe into learner corpora for error identification and adaptive feed- back provision. Silvia Pokrivcakova (2019) underscores the util- ity of AI and Natural Language Processing (NLP) in heightening the granularity of natural language descriptions, thereby height- ening corpus processing and elucidating the cognitive processes involved in human verbal communication. In addition, through multi- modal learning data analysis, AI constructs learner pro- files and dynamically optimises personalised learning pathways (Tu et al. 2025). AI- driven educational systems adeptly assess learners' linguistic outputs, discern individual learning require- ments and furnish real- time feedback to refine teaching strat- egies. In practical language instruction settings, AI platforms 

function as autonomous learning tools, delivering adaptive training round- the- clock, thereby empowering educators to concentrate on higher- level pedagogical responsibilities. This collaborative ‘human- computer’ approach is reshaping contem- porary language education practices (Zheng and Tang  2025). Last but not least, automated formative assessment systems monitor learning trajectories continuously, furnishing teachers with data- driven decision- making support (Xavier et al. 2025). To effectively harness the operational mechanisms and func- tionalities of the three AI technologies in language education, it is imperative to conduct in- depth exploration into AI's foun- dational principles and pragmatic implementations in this field.

The surge in AI research within language education has led to the emergence of Intelligent Computer- Assisted Language Learning (ICALL) as an extension of computer- assisted lan- guage learning (CALL) that incorporates AI (Choi  2014; Schulze 2008). As a prominent AI- driven approach in language teaching and learning, ICALL leverages various AI technol- ogies to facilitate sophisticated interactions between learners and the learning environment. For instance, NLP modules en- able multi- modal language interaction through technologies such as speech recognition and generation (e.g., chatbots), em- powering students to practice listening, speaking and reading skills in a simulated real- life language communication setting by providing real- time voice interaction and feedback (Kerins and Ramsay  2012). Learner modelling systems, underpinned by machine learning algorithms, continuously monitor individ- ual behavioural data (e.g., answer patterns, response duration) and employ immediate feedback mechanisms (e.g., Duolingo's error correction prompts) to develop dynamic cognitive maps encompassing language proficiency matrices, memory decay curves and learning style preferences. These models forecast individual learner performance to optimise content difficulty gradients and tailor instruction to individual needs (Kannan and Munday 2018; Ai 2017). In practical educational settings, numerous researchers have developed innovative instructional systems to establish ICALL environments through the integra- tion of AI. For instance, Huang and Wang (2021) incorporated an AI- based motion- aware teaching system tailored for vocab- ulary acquisition among second language (L2) French learners. This system provides students with real- time feedback by ana- lysing their gestures captured through a webcam to assess their comprehension levels. AI technologies can further strengthen student engagement by tapping into their existing knowledge base. Apart from that, the utilisation of AI- supported writing tools and automated essay grading software enables educators to assign writing tasks, offer learners feedback on grammar, spell- ing and mechanics (Dodigovic  2007; Huang and Tsao  2021), and automatically critique essays upon completion. These tools encompass functionalities such as precise error identification, categorization, underscoring and suggestions for revising vocab- ulary and grammatical mistakes within the original text.

As indicated by research (Silvia Pokrivcakova  2019), the ef- fectiveness of ICALL is hindered by teachers' technological readiness. Teachers encounter barriers in accepting AI sys- tems, primarily on account of concerns about the technology's perceived efficacy. For one thing, they worry that autonomous decision- making by the system or algorithms may diminish their pedagogical control. For another, their limited AI literacy 

results in undervaluing the tool's usefulness (Abdelhalim [2016;](#disclosure-permission-to-reproduce-material-from-other-sources-this-manu--script-does-not-include-any-material-reproduced-from-other-sources-re--quiring-permission) Park and Son  2009). To mitigate this limitation, it is crucial for system design to prioritise human- centered principles. Scholars emphasise the significance of teachers' beliefs, and preferences in the effectiveness of CALL methods (Straková and Cimermanová 2018). As a consequence, it is sensible to as- sume that teachers are more likely to integrate ICALL into their teaching practices if they receive proper training in AI technol- ogies and have affirmative AI- related experiences. Ensuring teachers are adequately prepared and confident to engage with AI technology- elevated environments is essential for successful implementation.

**2.2 \| AI Literacy**

As a cutting- edge form of digital literacy in the era of intelli- gence, AI literacy extends beyond mere technological manipu- lation. It encompasses a diverse spectrum of individual abilities for fostering effective interaction, critical reflection and collabo- rative innovation within an AI- integrated educational environ- ment (Long et al. 2021; Prior et al. 2016). The development of AI literacy is a progressive process rooted in the gradual acqui- sition of foundational knowledge and skills. Wang et al. (2023) defined AI literacy as the capacity to recognise and comprehend AI technologies in practical contexts, apply these technologies proficiently to accomplish tasks, and analyse, select and criti- cally evaluate data and information provided by AI systems, simultaneously cultivating a sense of personal responsibility and respect for mutual rights and obligations. Subsequent to the above steps, a comprehensive theoretical model of AI literacy is recommended on the basis of this definition, comprising four essential components, namely, awareness (recognising and un- derstanding AI technologies in AI- driven applications), applica- tion (effectively implementing AI technologies to complete tasks efficiently), evaluation (critically analysing, selecting and evalu- ating AI applications and their outcomes), and ethics (compre- hending the responsibilities and potential risks associated with the deployment and utilisation of AI technologies). AI literacy varies among individuals in dissimilar technological contexts. Wang et al. (2023) define AI literacy as comprising AI under- standing, awareness, application and ethics. Research suggests that proficiency in AI literacy reinforces professional adaptabil- ity and competitiveness in the global digital education landscape (Barkati et  al. 2024). For pre- service language educators, AI literacy entails comprehending technical aspects like machine learning algorithms and NLP, as well as critically evaluating the educational value of AI- generated content, adjusting strategies for human- computer collaboration, and upholding pedagogical subjectivity (Eguchi et al. 2021; Hermann 2022). The level of AI literacy among pre- service teachers strikingly influences their preparedness to incorporate AI technologies into future class- rooms. In this study, AI literacy denotes pre- service teachers' capacity to possess knowledge of AI, apply it in educational set- tings, and consider AI ethics.

While the significance of AI literacy is universally acknowl- edged, current research exhibits limitations, comprising a predominant revolve around student- centered AI liter- acy development and a deficiency in a cohesive pedagogical framework for AI literacy application research. In the field 

3 of 22

of language education, it is tremendously paramount to ac- knowledge factors that affect teachers' use of AI technology platforms. As put forward by Chiu et al. (2022), motivation facilitates teachers to design technology- supported teaching and augment their digital literacy. Shen and Cui (2024) estab- lished an affirmative association between need fulfilment and AI literacy in a study investigating the influence of psycho- logical need fulfilment on AI literacy among college students. The study aims to examine how pre- service teachers can proactively and effectively strengthen their utilisation of AI tools and software in teaching by integrating AI literacy into a motivation model driven by self- determination theory (SDT). This investigation not only elucidates the synergistic interplay between skill development and psychological drive but also identifies practical intervention strategies for heightening pre- service teacher education. This line of inquiry addresses an appeal in digital education research that, in an era featured by technological advancement, the cultivation of literacy should align with individuals' intrinsic motivation (Markauskaite et al. 2022).

**2.3 \| Teachers' AI Self- Efficacy (AI- TSE)**

Self- efficacy is a core concept put forth by Bandura  (1999), which emphasises the interaction among distinct individuals, social backgrounds and human behaviours. It refers to the indi- vidual's self- belief in the competence to complete a specific task (Cabir Hakyemez and Mardikyan 2021). This study investigates language teachers' self- efficacy in understanding and applying AI, particularly their perceived competence in mastering and implementing AI technologies (Chai et al. 2021).

Previous studies have identified specific self- efficacy as a cru- cial determinant in exploring an individual's inclination to- wards adopting and utilising technology (Yao and Wang 2024). Self- efficacy immensely affects individuals' willingness to learn and use AI. Individuals characterised by higher self- efficacy typically demonstrate more remarkable engagement and more intense behavioural intentions towards AI. For instance, pri- mary and secondary educators often report higher levels of AI self- efficacy, perceive AI's capacity to augment pedagogical out- comes, and consequently drive proactive adoption of these tech- nologies (Hsu et al. 2023). On top of that, Kong (2008) defines AI self- efficacy as an individual's confidence in the competence to complete AI- related tasks and their tendency to perform tasks. More importantly, this confidence is paramount to initiating and sustaining the utilisation of AI technology. In the field of computer education, Malmi et al. (2020) reviewed 50 relevant literature and found that 45% of the studies cited self- efficacy theory, which further underlined its significance in the accep- tance of educational technology.

Understanding the determinants of AI self- efficacy is essential for designing effective AI programs (Bewersdorff et al. 2025). Self- efficacy is intricately linked with cognitive, affective and behavioural factors (Eccles and Wigfield 2002), rather than de- veloping in isolation. Parsakia (2023) put forward a viewpoint that individuals proficient in technology use, encompassing AI, tend to exhibit higher levels of self- efficacy. Moreover, Anierobi et al. (2025) underscored the significance of psychological needs 

rooted in SDT in fostering intrinsic motivation, thereby height- ening academic self- efficacy, engagement and student satisfac- tion. On the basis of this framework, our study aims to explore the impact of psychological motivation on AI self- efficacy. In particular, existing research predominantly centers around assessing the direct influence of self- efficacy, with limited ex- ploration of its mediating role in the association between psy- chological motivation and technical behavioural intentions.

This paper extensively centres around the mediating role of AI self- efficacy between self- motivation factors and behavioural in- tentions, which is primarily intended to reveal its crucial influ- encing path on the acceptance of AI technology by pre- service language teachers.

**2.4 \| A Self- Determination Theory (SDT)**

As a foundational framework for understanding motivation, SDT emphasises the supporting role of three basic psychological needs, namely autonomy, competence and relevance, on intrin- sic motivation (Deci and Ryan 2000; Ryan and Deci 2017). In the field of education, SDT extends its application beyond explain- ing student motivation to encompass research on teacher profes- sional development and teaching innovation. Noels et al. (2019) put forth a standpoint that addressing these needs in language learning contexts conspicuously reinforces learners' engagement and sustained motivation. Within contemporary educational technology, SDT's explanatory framework continues to expand, particularly in analysing how digital tools mediate psycholog- ical need fulfilment in technology- elevated learning environ- ments. Furthermore, studies have illustrated that incorporating the principles of SDT into teacher training programmes can sub- stantially reinforce teachers' technology acceptance and their initiative in professional development. Gorozidis et  al.  (2020) successfully ameliorated the participation and teaching inno- vation of physical education teachers by satisfying their basic psychological needs when designing physical education teacher training. Likewise, Haukås et al. (2022) come up with an online language teacher education (OLTE) course grounded in the SDT framework and verified the effectiveness of SDT in heightening teachers' intrinsic motivation and professional development. In the AI era, the application of AI platforms or tools exemplifies specific teaching applications, such as leveraging intelligent teaching platforms to automatically evaluate students' home- work or utilising generative AI to produce oral and listening materials tailored to students' proficiency levels. These also put forward higher requirements and more specific subject adapt- ability for the AI literacy of language teachers (Sun et al. 2023). For this reason, it can be appropriately anticipated that there ex- ists a synergy between SDT and AI literacy. The psychological necessitates satisfaction in SDT provides the basis for intrinsic motivation, while AI literacy fosters teacher implementation at the behavioural level through skill reinforcement and teaching innovation. With SDT as the theoretical basis, the synergy of AI literacy can more effectively heighten the behavioural intentions of pre- service teachers in the educational context.

It is noteworthy that self- efficacy is inextricably linked to SDT theory. While self- efficacy holds a pivotal role across diverse research domains, it operates synergistically rather than in 

isolation. Prior studies have frequently examined its interplay with various theoretical frameworks, notably Causal Attributions (Weiner 1986) and Expectancy framework (Bandura, A., 1999); aside from that, self- efficacy is also associated with SDT (Deci and Ryan 2000), and is often confused with ‘perceptual ability’. On the basis of the previous definitions, both self- efficacy and perceptual ability emphasise the need for a sense of competence to be associated with worthwhile tasks and the centrality of per- sonal agency. This coincides with Bandura's (1999) notion of indi- vidual initiative as a crucial component of self- efficacy. Rodgers et al. (2014) in the sports setting also confirmed that perceptual ability is conceptualised within the conceptual framework of SDT, whereas self- efficacy is developed within the theoretical framework of social cognitive theory. In empirical educational research, we tried to elucidate the connection between teachers' SDT- related characteristics and AI self- efficacy.

To strengthen the effectiveness of pre- service language teachers' utilisation of the ICALL system, this study aims to integrate the technological rationale with teachers' psychological processes. Accordingly, the research commences by employing SDT to delve into educators' psychological requirements concerning AI applications in education and their associated motivational fac- tors. Autonomy refers to whether pre- service teachers can expe- rience the feeling of autonomous choice and autonomous control in the use of AI technology, a paramount factor influencing their behavioural intentions. As already suggested by certain studies, the experience of autonomy can substantially strengthen indi- viduals' innovative tendencies and adaptability to technology (Kusurkar et  al. 2013). The complexity of AI technology may pose a significant challenge to teachers' technical confidence, rendering satisfaction with competence to be tremendously par- amount. Teachers' proficiency in AI technology and their experi- ence of task success are considered pivotal factors in heightening their technology acceptance (Chai et al. 2021). Relevance refers to the sense of interaction and belonging between teachers and colleagues or learners when using AI technology, which can further support their motivation. As evidently demonstrated by associated studies, the social application scenarios of technology can conspicuously strengthen users' willingness to employ tech- nology (Ryan and Deci 2017).

This study aimed to probe into the determinants of pre- service teachers' behavioural intentions to utilise AI technology in their teaching practices. By examining the literature on SDT, AI self- efficacy and AI literacy, the study focused on autonomy, compe- tence, relevance, AI literacy and AI self- efficacy as paramount factors influencing pre- service teachers' behavioural intentions towards AI integration in teaching. The intricate interplay of these factors was analysed to gain insights into the complex adoption of AI in educational settings. The research findings, grounded in the developed model, offer valuable implications for designing effective AI training programs for pre- service teach- ers. The research questions addressed in this study are as follows:

**2.5 \| Research Questions**

1. Can autonomy, competence and relevance in the SDT theory predict the impact of AI literacy and self- efficacy among pre- service language teachers?
2. Can autonomy, competence and relevance in the SDT the- ory predict the impact of behavioural intentions to em- ploy AI for teaching and learning in pre- service language teachers?
3. Do pre- service teachers' AI literacy and AI self- efficacy play a mediating role between their perceptual autonomy, relevance, competence and behavioural intentions?

**3 \| Research Hypotheses and Model**

**3.1 \| Research Hypotheses**

**3.1.1 \| Perceptual Autonomy, Competence and Relevance Can Be Predictors of AI Self- Efficacy and AI Literacy**

Self- efficacy is intricately associated with SDT (Deci and Ryan  2000), particularly evident in the realms of kinesiology and physical education research. Rodgers et al. (2014) validated the distinction between perceived competence and self- efficacy within SDT in the field of kinesiology, supporting this differen- tiation conceptually and psychometrically. In the field of peda- gogy, Duchatelet and Donche (2019) underscored the interplay between autonomy, competence and self- perception, under- lining a direct correlation. Furthermore, Ghbari et  al.  (2024) demonstrated a connection between self- determination, self- efficacy and academic engagement, with results indicating the direct impact of autonomy and competence on self- efficacy. Building upon these existing studies, the present study formu- lates the following hypotheses:

**H1a.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual autonomy imposes a striking and positive impact on AI self- efficacy_.

**H1b.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual relevance has a substan-_ _tial and positive impact on AI self- efficacy_.

**H1c.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual competence has a dra-_ _matic and positive impact on AI self- efficacy_.

In current research on behavioural intentions, the TAM model has mostly been used to explore the role of psychologi- cal and self- efficacy elements of teachers on their behavioural intentions (An et al. 2023). These psychological elements have similar characteristics to SDT. According to research, in the realm of systems development, Wang et al. (2016) delved into the learning intentions of information systems developers with regard to business skills through the lens of Ryan and Deci's SDT. Their study underscored that the learning inten- tions of systems developers are influenced by both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, as well as by supportive working environments and perceived self- efficacy in learning. Chai et al. (2022) empirically demonstrate that the configuration of educational materials, autonomy and AI aimed at societal advancement can forecast individuals' behavioural inclina- tions towards learning AI. On this basis, we can anticipate that within the field of education, teachers' behavioural inten- tions are influenced by competence, autonomy and relevance in A SDT. On that account, this study predicts that pre- service 

5 of 22

teachers' psychological need for perceptual autonomy, com- petence and relevance affirmatively influence the variables correlated with AI use, and rooted in the aforementioned re- search, we formulate a few hypotheses:

**H2a.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual autonomy has a conspic-_ _uous and positive impact on their behavioural intentions to em-_ _ploy AI for teaching and learning_.

**H2b.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual relevance has a substan-_ _tial and positive impact on their behavioural intentions to utilise AI for teaching and learning_.

**H2c.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual competence has a striking and positive impact on their behavioural intentions to adopt AI for teaching and learning_.

SDT serves as a framework for understanding the development of individual AI literacy. Previous studies have demonstrated that satisfying autonomy and competence needs is crucial for heightening technology cognition and augmenting learning outcomes (Xia et  al.  2023). Specifically, individuals tend to perceive AI tools as more valuable and satisfying when these tools effectively address their needs (Panagoulias et al. 2024). Shen and Cui  (2024) have further supported this notion by confirming that autonomy and competence needs are strong predictors of AI literacy, directly influencing an individu- al's ability to navigate technological complexity. Moreover, Xia et al. (2022) have underlined that SDT reinforces learn- ers' technological readiness, boosts self- confidence, reduces anxiety and fosters intrinsic motivation. Thus, an affirmative correlation between need fulfilment and AI literacy can be in- ferred. Grounded in these findings, the following hypotheses are posited:

**H3a.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual autonomy has a remark-_ _able and positive impact on AI literacy_.

**H3b.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual relevance imposes a no-_ _ticeable and positive impact on AI literacy_.

**H3c.** _Pre- service teachers' perceptual competence exerts a strik-_ _ing and positive impact on AI literacy_.

**3.1.2** \| **AI Literacy Can Be an Indicator of AI Self- Efficacy**

The concept of AI self- efficacy is associated with the expecta- tions of pre- service teachers with regard to their ability to im- plement and plan for a wide spectrum of tasks that they need to complete in order to elevate their performance (Oran 2023). Sun et al. (202) utilised an experimental approach to demon- strate that teachers' AI self- efficacy augmented conspicu- ously after an experiment on augmenting competence in areas such as AI knowledge. Bećirović et al. (2025) dug into the impact of two distinct components of AI literacy, namely, technical comprehension of AI and its practical application, on AI self- efficacy, finding a substantial and positive correla- tion. Moreover, Getenet et al. (2024) have also confirmed the 

efficacy of digital literacy in heightening individual digital self- efficacy. Hornberger et al. (2023) studied the correlation of AI self- efficacy with AI literacy, and the results also demon- strated a striking and positive correlation between AI literacy and self- efficacy and interest. Bewersdorff et al. (2025) em- pirically validated a path model demonstrating how the use of AI, interest in AI and AI literacy collectively strengthen AI self- efficacy. As a consequence, this study come up with the following assumptions:

**H4.** _Pre- service teachers' AI literacy exerts a remarkable and positive impact on AI self- efficacy_.

**3.1.3** \| **AI Literacy Can Be an Indicator of Behavioural Intentions to Adopt AI for Teaching and Learning**

Current smart technologies are underutilised in education (Luckin et al. 2016). The integration of AI in education is an- ticipated to be significantly shaped by teachers' proficiency and expertise. Equipping educators with the requisite skills and knowledge to deploy AI- driven tools can substantially enhance instructional efficacy (Cavalcanti et  al.  2021). For instance, teachers' proficiency in AI can augment their ped- agogical skills and motivation, empowering them to strategi- cally integrate AI tools into classroom practices to enhance student engagement and learning drive (Wang et  al.  2021). Ismail Celik's (2023) study put forth a standpoint that incor- porating AI- EdTech in lessons hinges on teachers' pedagogical and technological expertise. Chai et al. (2021) study confirmed that AI literacy underlies ‘behavioral, normative, and control beliefs, thereby predicting BI (behavioral intentions)’. In a study of medical students' perceptions of AI and behavioural intentions, Li et al. (2022) put forth a viewpoint that when pos- sessing AI medical literacy, one is less likely to feel pressured to adopt AI technology in medical practice. In contrast, when not possessing AI medical literacy, one may experience greater societal pressure from conspicuous others when applying AI technology. This is also consistent with findings validated by Hornberger (Hornberger et al. 2023), demonstrating the conse- quences of AI literacy on behavioural intentions predictive as- sociation between them. Consequently, this study put forward the following hypotheses as follows:

**H5.** _Pre- service teachers' AI literacy exerts a remarkable and positive impact on their behavioural intentions to employ AI for teaching and learning_.

**5.1.2.3** \| **Exploratory Factor Analysis.** Herein, the ‘mini- mum residual extraction method’ and ‘oblique rotation method’ are adopted for exploratory factor analysis, involving six prin- cipal components. The specific factor analysis results and fac- tor loadings are revealed in Table 5.

The table above examines factor extraction and the proportion of information retained by the factors. It shows that all six- factor components exhibit loadings exceeding 0.5, confirming strong item- factor correlations. The majority of the unique residual val- ues range between 0.3 and 0.5, suggesting that each factor im- poses a favourable explanatory power for its items. Nevertheless, there is still a certain degree of uniqueness in the items.

Furthermore, an evaluation of the model fit from factor analy- sis is conducted to ascertain the plausibility of the factor model structure, its efficacy in elucidating the data, and its alignment with theoretical expectations.

Model fit evaluation is revealed in Table 6:

As suggested in the table, the RMSEA is 0.012, and the confi- dence interval is \[0.000, 0.019\], both lower than 0.05. Besides, the surface model fit is considerably satisfactory. The TLI is 0.993 (\> 0.90), close to 1, suggesting excellent model fit (Hara et al. 2010). The BIC is −3461, being negative, and the surface model imposes a desirable balance between complexity and fit. The _χ_2/df value of 718/660≈1.09 further suggests that the model is well- fitted to the data. A favourable fit is defined as having a minimum fit function (_χ_2) and a ratio of _χ_2 to its degree of free- dom (2/df) with a value less than 3.0 (Carmines and McIver 1981).

To sum up, the factor model demonstrates acceptable fit across all standard deviation metrics and satisfies the criteria for a sat- isfactory fit. For this reason, the model's results are deemed ac- ceptable and align with the goodness of fit evaluation standards commonly employed in academic research.

The validation factor analysis was principally to probe into the responses of the questionnaire grounded in a total of 43 items and six factors. This demon- strates that the analytical data is beneficial for convergent valid- ity (Teo and van Schaik 2012). The AVE calculation guarantees that each latent variable accounts for a minimum of 50% of the variance in its measurement index. Additionally, the CR value signifies that over 70% of the variance is attributed to the latent variable, thereby reinforcing the scale's internal consistency and measurement reliability.

To validate the scale's discriminant validity, the HTMT (Heterotrait- Monotrait Ratio of Correlations) ratio method was applied as the primary statistical tool in this study, which is an indicator for assessing the discriminant validity of reflec- tive constructs, particularly in structural equation modelling. In line with the recommendations of Henseler et al., HTMT values below 0.85 illustrate satisfactory discriminant validity between constructs (Henseler et al. 2015). Scale HTMT het- erogeneous–homogeneous ratio matrix is demonstrated in Table [9:](#behavioural)

**5.2 \| Structural Model**

**5.2.1 \| Hypothetical Modelling and Impact Analysis**

This paper centers around the direct effects of autonomy, rele- vance and competence on AI self- efficacy and AI literacy, the direct effects of AI literacy on AI self- efficacy, and behavioural intentions, the direct effects of AI self- efficacy on behavioural intentions, and the mediating effects of AI self- efficacy and AI literacy played by autonomy, relevance, competence on be- havioural intentions.

Its corresponding structural model diagram is illustrated in Figure [2:](#behavioural)

Substantial methodological distinctions exist between Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS- SEM) and covariance- based Structural Equation Modelling (CB- SEM). While CB- SEM employs model fit indices to assess the con- gruence between the data and the model, PLS- SEM prioritises the prediction and explication of variance in the dependent variable over the replication of the data's covariance matrix. Consequently, conventional model fit criteria are not suitable for assessing PLS- SEM (Henseler et al. 2016).

Its hypothesis model parameter test values are suggested in Table [10 ](#intentions)below:

As evidenced by our research findings, hypotheses  H1a–c, H2a–c, H4, H5 and H6 were supported without exception, while H2c was not supported. Perceived autonomy substantially in- fluenced AI literacy (_β_ = 0.221, _p_\< 0.001) and AI self- efficacy (_β_ = 0.143, _p_ \< 0.001), revealing that greater perceived autonomy and control over technology use by teachers led to higher tech- nological understanding and confidence. While the impact of perceived autonomy on behavioural intentions was weaker, it re- mained noticeable (_β_ = 0.078, _p_ = 0.020). Perceived competence had a remarkable and positive effect on AI literacy (_β_ = 0.112, _p_ = 0.007) and AI self- efficacy (_β_ = 0.081, _p_ = 0.012), but its di- rect influence on behavioural intentions demonstrated negligi- ble significance (_β_ = 0.047, _p_ = 0.118). Furthermore, perceived relevance positively affected AI literacy (_β_ = 0.152, _p_ \< 0.001), AI self- efficacy (_β_ = 0.109, _p_= 0.003) and behavioural inten- tions (_β_ = 0.084, _p_= 0.014), illustrating that social interactions and collaboration in technology elevated teachers' readiness to adopt it. The association between AI literacy and AI self- efficacy (_β_ = 0.498, _p_ \< 0.001) as well as behavioural intentions (_β_ = 0.224, _p_ \< 0.001) demonstrated strong and positive effects. In particu- lar, the direct impact of AI self- efficacy on behavioural inten- tion was striking (_β_ = 0.452, _p_ \< 0.001), underscoring the pivotal role of teachers' confidence in technology in decision- making processes.

**5.2.2** \| **Hypothesis Testing of Mediating Effects**

The mediating effect was tested by building a PLS- SEM model in Smartpls 4.0. The effect values of the model after 5000 opera- tions using Bootstrap algorithm are shown below Table [11:](#intentions)

To assess mediation in the model, mediation effect analysis was conducted on the variables. As demonstrated by the analytical outcomes, AI self- efficacy had a marked indirect effect (_p_ \< 0.05) on autonomy, relevance and competence on behavioural inten- tions, with effect values of 0.055, 0.042 and 0.031 respectively, demonstrating the presence of mediating effects. Their direct ef- fect values are demonstrated in the table of model parameter test values, which demonstrates that the direct effect of autonomy and relevance on behavioural intentions are both significant, while the type of mediation is partial mediation; the direct effect of competence on behavioural intentions are not significant, and the type of mediation is full mediation. Hypothesis H7 is sup- ported. The indirect effect of AI literacy on autonomy, relevance and competence on behavioural intentions are striking (_p_ \< 0.05) with effect values of 0.044, 0.030 and 0.022, respectively, which suggests that the mediating effect exists. Their direct effect val- ues are revealed in the table of model parameter test values, which suggests that the direct effect of autonomy and relevance on behavioural intentions are both significant, and the media- tion type is partial mediation; the direct effect of competence on behavioural intentions are not significant, and the mediation type is full mediation. Hypothesis H8 is supported.

Total effects and mediation effect proportions in the PLS- SEM model are shown below Table 12:

The above table presents the total effect path coefficients be- tween autonomy, relevance and competence and behavioural in- tentions. In particular, the mediating roles of AI self- efficacy and AI literacy within the model can be discerned by integrating the specific indirect effect values from the PLS- SEM path analysis. In particular, AI self- efficacy exhibits a higher mediating effect proportion compared to AI literacy, suggesting that the influence of autonomy, relevance and competence on behavioural inten- tions are more substantially mediated by AI self- efficacy than by AI literacy.

**6.1 \| The Influence of the Psychological Needs (Perceived Autonomy, Competence and Relevance) of Pre- Service Teachers on Their AI Literacy and AI Self- Efficacy**

For the psychological needs and personal motivation related hypotheses, that is, AI self- efficacy is substantially affected by autonomy (H1a), relevance (H1b) and competence (H1c); and AI literacy is substantially affected by autonomy (H3a), relevance (H3b) and competence (H3c). The study's results confirm that all six hypotheses received empirical support.

**6.1.1** \| **The Correlation Between Pre- Service Teachers' Psychological Needs (Perception of Autonomy, Competence and Relevance) and AI Literacy**

The study findings reveal that fulfilling the three identified needs (H3a–H3c) dramatically reinforces AI literacy. Improved satisfaction of pre- service teachers' autonomy, competence and relevance needs correlates with an affirmative impact on their AI literacy levels. As a consequence, heightening AI literacy among

pre- service teachers necessitates a comprehensive understand- ing of their psychological needs by governmental bodies and educational institutions. The outcomes of this study are com- patible with Chiu (2021) findings that students' active participa- tion in technology- infused environments can contribute to their 

literacy, which is pivotal for learning and cognitive processes. The current study's results suggest that the correlation with AI literacy may stem from a historical revolve around the cognitive aspects rather than the affective dimensions of the student- AI correlation. For educators, striking a balance between technol- ogy and interpersonal dynamics in teacher- student interactions is crucial. Fulfilling relevance needs can strengthen the social integration of technological tools, thereby heightening the effi- cacy of AI literacy initiatives.

**6.1.2** \| **The Correlation Between Pre- Service Teachers' Psychological Needs (Perception of Autonomy, Competence and Relevance) and AI Self- Efficacy**

The results indicated that fulfilling the three psychological needs (H3a–H3c) had a more affirmative impact on AI self- efficacy. These results align with Andrea Klaeijsen et  al.'s  (2018) study, which also found a remarkable connection between basic psycho- logical needs and occupational self- efficacy (H3). Duchatelet and Donche (2019) and Ghbari et al. (2024) have demonstrated the con- spicuous influence of autonomy and competence on self- efficacy. Ringeisen and Bürgermeister (2015) underscore in their study that the elements of SDT—autonomy, relevance and competence—play a pivotal role in fostering students' autonomous cognitive skills across a diverse array of settings. **6.2 \| The Influence of AI Literacy and AI Self- Efficacy on Pre- Service Language Teachers' AI Technology Use Behavioural Intentions**

Our research findings suggest dramatic and positive effects of AI literacy with behavioural intentions (H5); AI self- efficacy with behavioural intentions (H6).

The results indicating a substantial influence of AI literacy on AI self- efficacy (H4) align with previous studies by Chen et al. (2022) and Chai et al. (2021), who observed a notable impact of AI literacy on course satisfaction and willingness to engage in AI software development, particularly underscoring its strong association with self- efficacy. Thus, the acquisition of AI liter- acy conducts a pivotal role in heightening teachers' confidence in utilising AI technology. The ability of teachers to effectively manage AI tools stems from their understanding of AI concepts. In addition, Du et al. (2024) demonstrated that the AI literacy of K- 12 educators directly correlates with their self- efficacy in AI

learning. The intensifying significance of AI literacy in the AI era has given rise to a novel form of digital literacy that is poised to become a focal point in future smart educational paradigms. The true onset of the AI era hinges on educators' adept integra- tion of AI technologies into their pedagogical approaches. For this reason, a teacher AI literacy training program, centered on the integration of AI tools in education, must not only cater to the psychological requirements of prospective teachers but also underscore the tangible benefits and significance of leveraging such technologies, alongside heightening their own AI liter- acy. This emphasis is instrumental in motivating educators to incorporate AI tools into their teaching methodologies and in fostering the continual alignment of their literacy skills with the evolving educational landscape, thereby playing a pivotal role in the broader adoption of AI technologies in educational settings.

The findings reveal a substantial and positive impact of pre- service language teachers' AI self- efficacy on their behavioural intentions (H5). This association suggests that pre- service teachers with higher confidence in their AI capabilities are more inclined to incorporate AI tools into their teaching methodolo- gies (Kwak et al. 2022). which demonstrates that these psychological needs are crucial determinants in the formation of intentions for individual be- havioural selections. This corresponds with the research find- ings of Chiu (2021). In the context of AI courses, autonomy and social relevance dramatically predict students' learning behavioural intentions. This underlines the significance of de- signing curricula that support students' autonomous decision- making and foster social interaction, as well as significance of learning resources. In AI literacy training for pre- service lan- guage teachers, heightening teachers' autonomy (such as giving teachers the right to choose technology and teaching methods) and relevance (such as underscoring the connection between technology and their professional goals) can effectively bolster teachers' behavioural intentions towards AI technology. A di- verse array of AI applications facilitate meaningful interactions between language teachers and students, transcending tempo- ral and spatial constraints (Bibauw et al. 2022). Teachers are more inclined to adopt AI when they acknowledge its efficacy in educational contexts, as evidenced by Dai et al. (2020), who underscore the pivotal role of perceived AI relevance in shaping behavioural intentions.

**6.3.2** \| **Deconstruction of Intermediary Mechanism**

The present study illustrates that the association between per- sonal motivation and behaviour is actually a bridge and medi- ator between psychological needs and behavioural intentions. Personal motivation explains the mechanism or path of the cor- relation between pre- service teachers' psychological needs and their behavioural intentions to get involved. AI literacy and AI self- efficacy are variables that transmit the influence or explain the connection. As predictor variables, AI literacy and AI self- efficacy play a mediating role in the link between pre- service teachers' need satisfaction and their behavioural intentions to employ AI. AI self- efficacy (H7) and AI literacy (H8) indirectly predict pre- service teachers' behavioural intentions to em- ploy AI by satisfying their needs for autonomy, relevance and competence.

In this study, the subordinate influential factors of AI liter- acy included AI understanding, AI awareness, AI application and AI ethics. The investigation into teachers' AI literacy lev- els, framed within these perspectives, contributes to a holistic understanding of AI integration in education. While previous 

**Proportion of mediating effect**

research has demonstrated how explaining SDT demand sup- port affects AI learning at the secondary level (Xia et al. 2022); the impact of SDT demand fulfilment on digital literacy (Chiu et  al.  2022). These cases illustrate the efficacy of integrating SDT with complementary theoretical frameworks to elucidate teacher behaviour, though all rely on limited AI knowledge to assess AI- related motivations or behavioural intentions. This study's findings aim to bridge gaps in research on SDT- driven factors influencing AI adoption in educational contexts. The study utilised the SDT model and extended it to encompass the self- efficacy and AI literacy of teachers. The findings shed light on the paradox of why a multitude of teachers do not have much intention to act despite satisfying the appropriate psychological needs. This phenomenon can be attributed to teachers' concerns about emerging AI technologies. To put it another way, the gap between the cognitive, technological and practical behaviours of technology integration that are available. In practical terms, although there is a study exploring the implications of AI liter- acy for teacher education and teacher personal growth by 2024 (Sperling et al. 2024), few initiatives currently exist to integrate it into teacher education (TE) programs (Vazhayil et al. 2019). As a result, pre- service teachers currently lack systematic AI- related development to strengthen AI literacy. Our research contributes to the understanding of the dilemma by underscoring the signif- icance of AI literacy in the interaction between instructors' psy- chological needs, SDT and its impact on behavioural intentions, underscoring the role that AI literacy conducts in facilitating teachers' integration of AI into practice.

**7 \| Practical Advice**

For the time being, educational institutions ranging from pri- mary schools to universities in the majority of countries have incorporated AI courses tailored to students' abilities, aiming to cultivate talents capable of adapting to future AI developments. The cultivation of these talents requires a large number of ex- cellent teachers equipped with corresponding AI systematic knowledge reserves to satisfy various teaching demands. The conclusion of this study has proved that the satisfaction of the basic psychological needs of pre- service teachers can have a stronger impact on behavioural intentions through AI literacy and AI self- efficacy. On this basis, this study investigates strat- egies for harmonising AI integration and pedagogical enhance- ment by addressing teachers' psychological needs.

17 of 22

First, with an aim to meet the psychological motivation needs of language teachers, three time nodes can be set in the process of longitudinal teacher AI empowerment education and training (early, middle and late training). Meanwhile, questionnaires can assess teachers' psychological need satisfaction across stages (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and track corresponding shifts in behavioural intentions. This dynamic study can reveal the changes in teachers' psychological needs across dissimilar teaching tasks, allowing for corresponding adjustment of train- ing contents. Aside from that, in subsequent studies, supporting factors that affect the satisfaction of language teachers' psycho- logical motivation needs can be further explored to effectively heighten the participation of language teachers in AI empower- ment education in a targeted manner (Chiu et al. 2022). Teachers experience psychological safety, access suitable digital tools for secure teaching, engage in collaborative sharing of practices and undertake reflective analysis of their experiences (Gorozidis and Papaioannou 2014).

In language education, developing pre- service teachers' AI lit- eracy and self- efficacy hinges on fulfilling psychological needs that integrate pedagogical technology and subject- matter exper- tise. The first involves the principle of autonomy. A multi- level AI training course allows pre- service teachers to select modules aligned with their capabilities, thereby heightening their mo- tivation to learn and their sense of autonomy in AI decision- making processes. Simultaneously, the evaluation and feedback ability of teachers themselves is also emphasised in the cultiva- tion of AI literacy (Tenberga and Daniela 2024). Incorporating simulated classrooms and authentic teaching tasks into training enables real- time feedback, facilitating teachers' translation of knowledge into practical skills. For competence development, fostering proficiency in language instruction, digital tool inte- gration and reflective practice is pivotal for seamlessly embed- ding AI technology into pedagogy and optimising. Finally, in terms of relevance support, trust and collaboration can be es- tablished through fixed group cooperation tasks and teaching seminars. Aside from that, strengthening teachers' connections to course content and collaborative teams reinforces overall psychological need satisfaction. These findings emphasise the necessity of reinforcing teachers' cognitive AI literacy and ap- plication confidence by addressing their psychological motiva- tions, thereby amplifying their behavioral intentions.

**8 \| Theoretical and Practical Implications**

This study synthesises psychological motivation with AI skill dimensions, offering empirical validation for AI applications in language education. By applying SDT to AI- elevated educa- tional contexts, it examines how fulfilling psychological needs influences teachers' intentions to adopt AI technologies. As a whole, this study fills the gap in the SDT framework to support teachers' professional growth in the digital education transfor- mation, adds a psychological perspective to the field of AI edu- cation applications, and reveals the paramount role of demand support policies in teachers' professional development. More importantly, the identification of pivotal factors influencing language teachers' behavioural intentions to adopt AI in teach- ing forges a theoretical foundation for the formulation of more 

targeted language pre- service education training content in the future.

During the study, it is essential to address the research's lim- itations and outline potential future research directions. To begin with, the reliance on teachers' self- reports for the results pertaining to SDT and personal motivation introduces poten- tial biases as a consequence of subjective perceptions and social desirability bias inherent in self- reported data. Future investi- gations could employ alternative methodologies such as online learning observations and interviews to corroborate the out- comes. In addition, this study exclusively examines psychologi- cal and personal motivators influencing behaviour, warranting exploration of external and other relevant motivational factors. Moreover, the examination of AI literacy in its entirety without dissecting its specific dimensions like technical manipulation skills and instructional design skills hinders a comprehensive understanding of how these dimensions relate to psychological needs fulfilment. Subsequent research could elucidate these links to inform targeted training approaches. Last but not least, while the study employed robust statistical techniques like Bootstrap mediation tests and theory- driven path modelling (Deci and Ryan 2000) to strengthen the explanatory power of variable associations, the cross- sectional survey design and ab- sence of longitudinal data constrain the ability to draw causal inferences with certainty. Furthermore, the sample predomi- nantly comprised pre- service language teachers, potentially im- pacting the generalizability of the results to other educational contexts.
